rows.question: For this project, how low can we make the ceilings in the retail sales area and the community-facility offices?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

For this project, how low can we make the ceilings in the retail sales area and the community-facility offices?

Research complete
01:04

The supported minimum is 7 feet 6 inches if the retail sales area and community-facility offices are occupiable rather than habitable spaces; habitable rooms and spaces require 8 feet. The code definitions needed to resolve that distinction for these uses are not included, so I cannot yet give an unconditional project minimum. Measure from the finished floor to the finished underside of the ceiling or ceiling beams. (2022 NYC BC § 1208.2)

For a furred ceiling in a nonhabitable room, the required minimum must be maintained over at least two-thirds of the room’s area; the remaining portion may be lower, but never below 7 feet. The exception preserves the § 1208.2 minimum for habitable rooms and spaces—this is not permission to lower their ceilings to 7 feet. (BC § 1208.2.1)

A separate exception permits 7-foot ceilings above and below a mezzanine, other than in habitable spaces; no mezzanine arrangement has been established for these areas. (BC § 1208.2, Exception 4)

Yes, conditionally: if the ductwork enclosure is a furred ceiling and the retail sales area is a nonhabitable occupiable space, your layout satisfies this ceiling-height rule. The required 7-foot-6-inch height would remain over 75% of the room’s area—more than the required two-thirds—and the lowered quarter would meet the 7-foot absolute minimum for a furred ceiling. (2022 NYC BC §§ 1208.2, 1208.2.1)

If the space is habitable, the furred-ceiling exception preserves the 8-foot minimum, so neither proposed height satisfies that requirement. rows.question: Could a café tenant keep propane cylinders outside this building? What fire-safety restrictions should we check before drawing a storage cage?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

Could a café tenant keep propane cylinders outside this building? What fire-safety restrictions should we check before drawing a storage cage?

Research complete
02:06

Possibly, but for your proposed mixed-use building with residential use, outdoor café cylinders larger than 16.4 ounces require commissioner authorization—even outside on the lot—and the storage facility itself must be approved. A cage does not by itself establish permission. The residential-lot restriction applies to any lot containing a building used for residential occupancy; containers over 16.4 ounces also cannot be brought into a nonresidential building without authorization. (FC §§ 6105.3(3), (5), (6), 6109.1)

Before drawing the cage, check:

Cylinder and total limits: No individual LPG container may have a capacity greater than 100 pounds. Outdoor storage is limited to 400 pounds of LPG total. These are separate limits, not alternatives. (FC §§ 6105.3(1), 6109.12)
Basic location: Storage must be at or above grade, not on a roof, and at least 20 feet from building openings, 20 feet from motor-vehicle fuel dispensers, and 10 feet from combustible material. Do not store or leave cylinders unattended near exit-access doors, exits, stairs, exit-discharge areas or other means of egress. (FC §§ 6109.4, 6109.6, 6109.12)
Additional exposure setbacks: For storage over 100 pounds through 400 pounds, Table 6109.12 requires, among other applicable exposures, 25 feet from subway openings and Group A occupancies/public gathering places, 10 feet from combustible-construction buildings, public sidewalks, parked vehicles, streets, private roads and lot lines, and 5 feet from air-compressor intakes or HVAC inlets. Other nearby hazardous-material storage must be checked against its specific table row. Only entries marked with footnote a qualify for reduction to 5 feet: a protective structure rated at least 2 hours must interrupt the line of sight, stand at least 5 feet from the exposure, and allow natural ventilation preventing hazardous gas accumulation. An ordinary cage is not that protective structure. (FC Table 6109.12 and note a)
Failure hazards: Do not locate storage where failure of structures or containment systems would expose the LPG to electric power lines or piping containing flammable/combustible liquids, flammable gases or oxidizing materials. (FC § 6109.12.1)
Enclosure and cylinder protection: Provide a suitable enclosure or other protection against tampering; minimize physical damage and excessive temperature rise, and provide vehicular protection as required by the commissioner. Stored outlet valves must be closed, with screw-on caps or collars securely installed whether cylinders are full, partly full or empty. Cylinders over 1 pound must be positioned with the pressure-relief valve communicating directly with the vapor space. (FC §§ 6109.2, 6109.3, 6109.8, 6109.13)
Electrical equipment: Except as otherwise provided in NFPA 58, equipment within 3 feet in any direction must meet Electrical Code Class I, Division 2 wiring requirements, unless separated by a wall or solid partition without openings. (FC § 6109.14)
Storage versus connected use: If cylinders supply a stationary LPG installation, access to public-utility piped natural gas prohibits that installation unless authorized by the commissioner. Equipment must be approved for LPG. (FC §§ 6105.1, 6105.3(10))

The cylinder capacities, total quantity, intended connection to café equipment, measured site clearances and commissioner authorization remain unresolved. A permit is required above the quantities referenced in FC § 105.6, but that provision is not available here, so the permit threshold cannot yet be determined. The NFPA 58 electrical exception also cannot be evaluated from the available text.

What cylinder size and maximum number of cylinders does the café propose to keep outside?

rows.question: What do we need to prevent scalding at the lavatory in the ground-floor public restroom?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

What do we need to prevent scalding at the lavatory in the ground-floor public restroom?

Research complete
00:32

The supplied code text does not establish what temperature limit or protective device is required to prevent scalding at this lavatory. It specifies maximum flow rates for public lavatories—0.25 gallon per metering cycle for metering faucets, or 0.5 gpm at 60 psi for other faucets—but those are flow limits, not scald-prevention requirements (PC § 604.4, Table 604.4).

rows.question: The central water heater would be set to 110°F. Can we rely on its thermostat and leave out the temperature-limiting device at the lavatory?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

What do we need to prevent scalding at the lavatory in the ground-floor public restroom?

Research complete
00:32

The supplied code text does not establish what temperature limit or protective device is required to prevent scalding at this lavatory. It specifies maximum flow rates for public lavatories—0.25 gallon per metering cycle for metering faucets, or 0.5 gpm at 60 psi for other faucets—but those are flow limits, not scald-prevention requirements (PC § 604.4, Table 604.4).

The central water heater would be set to 110°F. Can we rely on its thermostat and leave out the temperature-limiting device at the lavatory?

Research complete
00:55

No—if this restroom is provided for customers, patrons and visitors, the central heater’s 110°F thermostat setting cannot replace the required temperature-limiting device. The 2022 NYC Plumbing Code prohibits using a water-heater thermostat as the means of complying with maximum fixture delivery temperatures (PC § 607.1.1). For lavatories in those public toilet facilities, tempered water must be delivered through an approved device conforming to ASSE 1070. The exception covers point-of-use heaters with outlet temperature regulated to provide tempered water, not the proposed central heater (PC § 416.5).

The remaining applicability question is who the public restroom serves; “public restroom” alone does not establish the specific users named in § 416.5.

Will this restroom serve customers, patrons or visitors?

rows.question: For the fire department connection on the street wall, what clear space do we need to leave around it?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

For the fire department connection on the street wall, what clear space do we need to leave around it?

Research complete
00:34

Leave and maintain a clear working space at least 36 inches wide, 36 inches deep, and 78 inches high in front of and to the sides of the wall-mounted Fire Department connection (NYC Building Code § 912.4.2). The Fire Commissioner may require or approve otherwise; immediate access must also remain unobstructed (NYC Fire Code §§ 912.3, 912.3.2).

rows.question: Could a planter leave only 24 inches in front of it if the hose couplings are still visible?
rows.visibleText:
RESEARCH

History
⋯

For the fire department connection on the street wall, what clear space do we need to leave around it?

Research complete
00:34

Leave and maintain a clear working space at least 36 inches wide, 36 inches deep, and 78 inches high in front of and to the sides of the wall-mounted Fire Department connection (NYC Building Code § 912.4.2). The Fire Commissioner may require or approve otherwise; immediate access must also remain unobstructed (NYC Fire Code §§ 912.3, 912.3.2).

Could a planter leave only 24 inches in front of it if the hose couplings are still visible?

Research complete
00:41

No—unless the Fire Commissioner requires or approves a different clearance. For the wall-mounted fire department connection discussed, the required working space is at least 36 inches wide, 36 inches deep and 78 inches high, maintained in front of and to the sides (2022 NYC Building Code § 912.4.2). A planter leaving only 24 inches of depth falls 12 inches short; visible hose couplings do not substitute for working clearance.

Immediate access must also remain unobstructed, and the Fire Code independently requires the same working-space dimensions, subject to its stated exception for otherwise required or approved space (2022 NYC Fire Code, current consolidated text, §§ 912.3 and 912.3.2).
